options.text: They build complex molecules and reproduce rapidly

options.text: The milk stays sweeter for longer

Fast growth helps the culture, not sterility.

options.text: The amount of useful chemical produced climbs quickly

questions.stem: Why might a factory prefer bacterial production to chemical synthesis?

options.text: Bacteria can produce complex molecules that are hard to synthesise artificially
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Cultures need vessels and controls.
Yoghurt certainly spoils.

questions.stem: State the substance that bacteria added to milk can produce enzymes for.
questions.modelAnswer: Bacteria added to milk secrete enzymes that convert the milk into yoghurt.

questions.stem: Name the two bacterial talents that suit food production.
questions.modelAnswer: Bacteria produce complex molecules and they reproduce rapidly, raising output quickly.

questions.stem: Explain why rapid reproduction matters as much as product chemistry.
questions.modelAnswer: A process only pays if output scales, and fast division grows the producing population quickly, so the complex molecules accumulate at industrial speed.

questions.stem: A dairy wants faster yoghurt throughput. Apply the two bacterial advantages to suggest an approach.
questions.modelAnswer: Start with a larger healthy Lactobacillus culture, since rapid reproduction will expand it quickly, and the complex-molecule machinery will convert more lactose per hour.

options.text: To add calcium to the milk

Water content is unchanged.

options.text: The low pH suppresses harmful microbes and preserves the product longer

Acidity sours, it does not sweeten.

questions.stem: State the temperature range used to incubate the yoghurt culture.
questions.modelAnswer: The mixture is incubated at 40-45°C after the Lactobacillus is added.

questions.stem: Name the sugar that Lactobacillus converts into lactic acid.
questions.modelAnswer: Lactose, the milk sugar, is converted by Lactobacillus into lactic acid.

questions.stem: Explain why contamination before culturing would damage the yoghurt batch.
questions.modelAnswer: Unwanted bacteria would compete with Lactobacillus for the lactose, slowing production, and could spoil the taste of the finished yoghurt.

questions.stem: A batch turns out runny instead of thick. Apply the process chemistry to propose a cause.
questions.modelAnswer: Too little lactic acid likely formed, perhaps from a culture added before the milk reached 40-45°C or an incubation cut short, so the lactose never fully converted and the milk never thickened.
